title: Accuracy of online discussion forums on common childhood ailments
screen_reason: CONTENT prevalence: the share of parenting-forum health advice that was refuted or somewhat refuted when checked against evidence-based point-of-care resources is reported separately for each of the two forums, with denominators (16.2% and 6.3%). The paper explicitly frames this as whether the forums are 'an avenue for misinformation'.

estimates.country: Not stated (US-based public parenting websites; author based in Canada)
estimates.measure_type: % of advice-giving forum responses whose advice was refuted or somewhat refuted by evidence-based point-of-care resources
estimates.value_raw: 16.2% of advice on BabyCenter.com (of the 74 of 113 responses that provided advice)
estimates.denominator: 74 advice-providing responses on BabyCenter.com (the 65.5% of the 113 responses to the 74 health-related questions that offered advice)
estimates.definition: Each piece of advice was searched in DynaMed, UpToDate, RxTx and Natural Medicines and coded Supported / Somewhat supported / Refuted / Somewhat refuted / No evidence found; the numerator combines Refuted (fully refuted by evidence) and Somewhat refuted (partially refuted by evidence)
estimates.misinfo_def: “Refuted R Advice was fully refuted by evidence” / “Somewhat refuted SR Advice was partially refuted by evidence” (Table 1); the study asks “whether or not these forums are an avenue for misinformation”
estimates.source_quote: A further 16.2% and 6.3% was refuted or was somewhat refuted by the evidence found in evidence-based resources.
estimates.page_loc: Abstract, Results (quoted); same figure in the Results text, p. 460; denominator on p. 458 (“Of the 113 responses, 74 (65.5%) provided advice”)
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Single researcher (a health sciences librarian, the sole author) coded all responses by content analysis and judged each piece of advice against four evidence-based point-of-care resources (DynaMed, UpToDate, RxTx, Natural Medicines). No inter-rater reliability: 'the data analysis was performed by one researcher; therefore, there was no inter-rater reliability in the coding of responses', although a small set was recoded by the author for consistency. The author notes a physician reviewer would have been preferable.
estimates.moderator_quote: All questions in a six-month time period (June 2016-November 2016) that had at least one answer were extracted and used for data analysis. ... Any answers that provided advice were then searched in evidence-based, point-of-care resources to determine if the advice was supported or refuted by the evidence provided.
estimates.notes: Data from the two forums were explicitly NOT pooled ('data from different forums could not be pooled and were analyzed separately'), so this is one of two rows. Coincidence worth flagging: BabyCenter had 74 health-related questions AND 74 advice-providing responses; the denominator here is the 74 RESPONSES. The abstract loosely says '65.5% ... of the health-related questions' provided advice, but the Results make clear the denominator is the 113 responses. Confidence medium: single-coder judgement with no reliability statistic, and 'No evidence found' advice stays in the denominator (23% of BabyCenter advice), which deflates the falsity share relative to a verifiable-only denominator. QUOTE NOTE: the body sentence “Only 16.2% and 6.3% of advice on BabyCenter.com and WhattoExpect.com, respectively, was refuted or somewhat refuted by the medical evidence found in evidence-based resources” (p. 460) states the same values but is interleaved with the second column in the PDF text layer, so the equivalent abstract sentence is quoted instead as a contiguous verbatim span.

estimates.notes: Second of the two non-poolable forum rows. Same instrument and coder as the BabyCenter row, so the two are directly comparable to each other but were kept separate by the author because the forums' post structures forced different extraction methods. Limitation stated by the author: WhattoExpect.com was missing two months of posts for one of the five sections. 'No evidence found' advice (25% here) remains in the denominator. QUOTE NOTE: the body sentence “Only 16.2% and 6.3% of advice on BabyCenter.com and WhattoExpect.com, respectively, was refuted or somewhat refuted by the medical evidence found in evidence-based resources” (p. 460) states the same values but is interleaved with the second column in the PDF text layer, so the equivalent abstract sentence is quoted instead as a contiguous verbatim span.

missed_or_uncertain: Numbers seen but NOT extracted. (a) Agreement shares - 54.1% and 47.2% of advice agreed (or somewhat agreed) with the evidence - are the complement side of the same coding and measure accuracy, not misinformation; keeping them would double-count the same cell. (b) 'No evidence found' shares (23% and 25%) are unverifiable advice, not falsity. (c) Per-topic S/SS/R/SR/NEF counts in Table 4 (bowel movements, reflux, cold/congestion, rash/eczema, fever, by forum) would let one compute topic-level refuted shares, but every such value would be a cross-category sum I computed rather than a verbatim figure, so R8 forbids them; they are also thin (single digits per cell). (d) Discussion-text topic figures - bowel movements 'more than half (66%) agreed with the medical evidence, while only 16% disagreed'; common cold/congestion 90% agreed, 5% disagreed; rash/eczema 55% agreed - are verbatim, but their denominators (e.g. '61 responses that provided advice about bowel movements') pool the two forums, which the author says cannot be pooled, and they are demographic-style subgroup detail rather than the headline; per the 'keep the main figure' rule I left them out. (e) Response-type shares (26.5% suggested seeking medical attention, 23.0% offered a diagnosis on BabyCenter; 13.7% and 8.8% on WhattoExpect) are behaviour categories, not veracity. JUDGEMENT CALL for an adjudicator: this is CONTENT rather than QUALITY because advice was judged against an external ground truth (four evidence-based point-of-care resources) and explicitly labelled refuted, i.e. inaccurate - not scored on a completeness or readability instrument. breadth is coded 'misleading' because the verbatim 16.2%/6.3% numerator merges fully refuted with partially refuted advice; a fully-refuted-only share is not reported for either forum.

rob.design: Cross-sectional content analysis of two public parenting discussion forums. Forum selection: five typical childhood-ailment scenarios were googled with cleared history/cache, all forums appearing in the first five pages were recorded (18 forums), and the 2 meeting the inclusion criteria (public, no login, aimed at parents, posts by the general public, a children's health section) were used: BabyCenter.com and WhattoExpect.com. Census of all questions with at least one answer over June-November 2016, extracted by manual copy-paste: 492 questions / 777 responses (BabyCenter) and 587 questions / 3,445 responses (WhattoExpect), of which 74 and 131 questions were health-related. Content analysis and evidence checking by the single author, a health sciences librarian; NO inter-rater reliability statistic (a small set was self-recoded for consistency). Not a survey, so no response rate. Author-stated limitations: single coder, no clinician involved in the accuracy judgements, and two months of posts missing for one WhattoExpect.com section.
